newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Bosnia war crimes suspects "on notice", says U.S..
newsitem.headline: Bosnia war crimes suspects "on notice", says U.S..

text.p: The raid by NATO troops against two suspected war criminals in Bosnia has put others on notice they will not remain free indefinitely, U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen said on Thursday.

"I think all who are subject to indictment by the War Crimes Tribunal should be on notice that at some point in time that they will be brought to justice," Cohen told reporters when asked if indicted former Serb President Radovan Karadzic and others should take heed from the Thursday's action.

But he also said during a visit to Hungary that the move, which resulted in the arrest of one suspect and shooting dead of another by British troops, was not a direct result of a stern warning issued at a NATO summit in Madrid this week to former warring factions in Bosnia.

"There has been no political decision made to use the (military arrest) authority that has not been used in the past," Cohen told reporters, referring to reports of military reluctance to arrest suspects during encounters in the course of normal duties.
"I believe that there is no connection between the statment in Madrid and this... this is not directly related to the Madrid communique," he said.

Cohen said he had been aware of the pending actions and that a decision was made several days ago. He said U.S. forces provided logistical support and military backup for the British move in the British sector of Bosnia but did not take part in the arrest.

"I have not issued any such instructions and I do not believe any such instructions have been issued," Cohen replied when asked if he had given orders to U.S. peacekeeping troops in Bosnia to more actively go after indicted suspects who they might run across in the normal performance of their military duties.
Cohen said military leaders made the judgment that the two men involved in Thursday's incident could be arrested with minimal risk to troops.
"Obviously, a judgment was reached that, tactically and operationally, the time was right and appropriate for them to conduct a mission with minimum risk," he said.
"It was a tactical decision and that has to be a decision really made by the military authorities involved. They made such an assessment and obviously were successful."
"The United States did, in fact, provide logistical support and backup support, and (U.S. troops) were not participants in the arrest," he added.

Senior officials travelling with Cohen told reporters that a U.S. military C-130 aircraft was used to fly the arrested suspect, Milan Kovacevic, from Tuzla in Bosnia to the Hague to face legal action by the tribunal.

In a another separate action in the vicinity of Prijedor in Bosnia, suspected war criminal Simo Drljaca was shot dead. NATO said that Drljaca, the former police chief in Prijedor, opened fire on troops as they approached and challenged him for the purpose of detaining him.
One soldier was wounded in the process, NATO said.
